title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Shortly after nine that evening, Weyrother arrived at Kutuzov's quarters with his plans for the council of war. All the column commanders had been summoned, and all except Prince Bagration, who declined to attend, were there at the appointed time.

Weyrother, who was fully in charge of the planned battle, presented a sharp contrast in his eagerness and energy to the dissatisfied and drowsy Kutuzov, who reluctantly played the role of chairman. Weyrother was clearly aware he was driving a movement that had already become unstoppable. He was like a horse harnessed to a heavy cart running downhill — whether he was pulling it or being pushed by it, he couldn't tell, but he rushed forward at breakneck speed with no time to think about where this was all heading. He had been to the enemy's picket line twice that evening to scout in person, twice to the Russian and Austrian Emperors to report and explain, and to his own headquarters where he had dictated the battle plan in German. Now, thoroughly exhausted, he arrived at Kutuzov's.

He was so preoccupied that he forgot even basic courtesy toward the commander in chief. He interrupted him, spoke rapidly and indistinctly without looking at the person he was addressing, and ignored questions put to him. He was spattered with mud and had a harried, exhausted, distracted look about him, though at the same time he was arrogant and self-assured.

Kutuzov was occupying a modest nobleman's manor near Ostralitz. In the large drawing room that had become the commander in chief's office, Kutuzov himself, Weyrother, and the other council members had gathered. They were drinking tea and waiting only for Prince Bagration to begin. Finally Bagration's orderly arrived with the news that the prince could not attend. Prince Andrew came in to report this to the commander in chief and, having previously received Kutuzov's permission to attend the council, remained in the room.
"Since Prince Bagration isn't coming, we may as well begin," said Weyrother, hurriedly rising and going to the table where an enormous map of the area around Brunn was spread out.

Kutuzov, his uniform unbuttoned so that his thick neck bulged over his collar as though trying to escape, sat almost asleep in a low chair, his pudgy old hands resting symmetrically on the armrests. At the sound of Weyrother's voice, he opened one eye with effort.
"Yes, yes, go ahead. It's already late," he said, and nodding his head he let it droop and closed his eye again.

If at first the council members thought Kutuzov was only pretending to sleep, the sounds that soon came from his nose proved that the commander in chief was absorbed by something far more pressing than any desire to show his contempt for the battle plan or anything else — he was satisfying the irresistible human need for sleep. He was genuinely asleep. Weyrother, with the manner of a man too busy to waste a single moment, glanced at Kutuzov, confirmed he was asleep, picked up a paper, and in a loud, monotonous voice began reading out the battle plan, starting with its title:
"Dispositions for an attack on the enemy position behind Kobelnitz and Sokolnitz, November 30, 1805."
The dispositions were extremely complicated and difficult to follow. They began:

"Since the enemy's left wing rests on wooded hills and his right extends along Kobelnitz and Sokolnitz behind the ponds there, while we on the other hand far outflank his right with our left wing, it is advantageous to attack the enemy's right wing, especially if we occupy the villages of Sokolnitz and Kobelnitz, whereby we can both strike his flank and pursue him across the plain between Schlappanitz and the Thuerassa forest, avoiding the defiles of Schlappanitz and Bellowitz that cover the enemy's front. To this end it is necessary that... The first column marches... The second column marches... The third column marches..." and so on, Weyrother read.

The generals appeared to listen reluctantly to the complicated orders. The tall, fair-haired General Buxhowden stood leaning against the wall, his eyes fixed on a burning candle, seeming not to listen — or even wanting to be thought to listen. Directly opposite Weyrother sat the ruddy-faced Miloradovich, holding a military pose with his elbows out, hands on his knees, and shoulders raised, his glistening wide eyes fixed on Weyrother and his mustache twisted upward. He remained stubbornly silent, staring at Weyrother's face, and only looked away when the Austrian chief of staff finished reading. Then Miloradovich glanced around meaningfully at the other generals, though it was impossible to tell from that look whether he agreed or disagreed, was satisfied or not. Beside Weyrother sat Count Langeron, who wore the subtle smile that never left his typically southern French face throughout the entire reading, as he gazed at his slender fingers rapidly spinning a gold snuffbox adorned with a portrait. Midway through one of the longest sentences, he stopped spinning the snuffbox, raised his head, and with a thin-lipped smile of hostile politeness tried to interrupt Weyrother to make a point. But the Austrian general, still reading, frowned angrily and jerked his elbows, as if to say: "You can share your views later — for now, kindly look at the map and listen." Langeron raised his eyebrows in confusion, glanced at Miloradovich as if seeking support, but meeting the latter's impressive yet meaningless gaze, he dropped his eyes sadly and went back to spinning his snuffbox.
"A geography lesson!" he muttered, seemingly to himself but loud enough for everyone to hear.

Przhebyshevsky, with respectful but dignified politeness, cupped his hand to his ear toward Weyrother, with the air of a man deeply absorbed in concentration. Dokhturov, a small man sitting opposite Weyrother, leaned over the spread-out map with a conscientious and modest expression, earnestly studying the battle plan and the unfamiliar terrain. He asked Weyrother several times to repeat words he hadn't caught clearly and the difficult names of villages. Weyrother obliged, and Dokhturov noted them down.

When the reading — which lasted more than an hour — was over, Langeron set down his snuffbox again and, without looking at Weyrother or anyone in particular, began explaining how difficult it would be to carry out such a plan when the enemy's position was only assumed and not actually known, since the enemy might well be on the move. Langeron's objections were valid, but it was clear that his main purpose was to show General Weyrother — who had read his plan with the self-assurance of a teacher lecturing schoolchildren — that he was not dealing with fools, but with men who could teach him a thing or two about military affairs.

When the monotonous drone of Weyrother's voice stopped, Kutuzov opened his eye the way a miller wakes up when the soothing hum of the mill wheel suddenly stops. He listened to Langeron's remarks as if to say, "So you're still going on with this nonsense!" then quickly closed his eye again and let his head sink even lower.

Langeron, trying as sharply as possible to wound Weyrother's pride as the plan's author, argued that Bonaparte might easily attack rather than be attacked, which would make the entire plan worthless. Weyrother met every objection with a firm, contemptuous smile, clearly having prepared responses to any possible criticism.
"If he could have attacked us, he would have done so today," he said.
"So you think he's powerless?" said Langeron.
"He has forty thousand men at most," Weyrother replied, with the smile of a doctor whose elderly patient is trying to tell him how to treat the case.
"In that case he's practically inviting his own destruction by waiting for our attack," said Langeron with a subtly mocking smile, again glancing around at Miloradovich for support.
But Miloradovich was obviously thinking about anything other than what the generals were arguing about.
"Well!" he said. "Tomorrow we'll see it all on the battlefield."

Weyrother again gave that smile that seemed to say he found it both strange and absurd to face objections from Russian generals and to have to prove things he had already convinced not just himself of, but the Emperors as well.

"The enemy has put out his fires and there's a constant noise coming from his camp," he said. "What does that mean? Either he's retreating — which is the only thing we need to worry about — or he's changing position." He smiled knowingly. "But even if he also takes up a position in the Thuerassa, he merely saves us a great deal of trouble, and all our plans down to the smallest detail remain the same."
"How is that..." Prince Andrew began. He had been waiting a long time for a chance to voice his doubts.
But at that moment Kutuzov woke up, coughed heavily, and looked around at the generals.

"Gentlemen, the plans for tomorrow — or rather for today, since it is past midnight — can no longer be changed," he said. "You have heard them, and we shall all do our duty. But before a battle, there is nothing more important..." He paused. "...than a good night's sleep."
He moved as if to stand. The generals bowed and withdrew. It was past midnight. Prince Andrew went out.

The council of war, at which Prince Andrew had not managed to express the opinion he'd hoped to share, left him with a vague, uneasy feeling. Whether Dolgorukov and Weyrother were right, or Kutuzov, Langeron, and the others who opposed the plan of attack — he couldn't tell. "But was it really impossible for Kutuzov to speak plainly to the Emperor? Is it possible that because of court politics and personal considerations, tens of thousands of lives — and my life, my life," he thought, "must be put at risk?"

"Yes, it's very likely that I'll be killed tomorrow," he thought. And suddenly, at this thought of death, a whole series of distant, deeply personal memories rose in his mind: he remembered his last farewell to his father and his wife; he remembered the early days when he first loved her. He thought about her pregnancy and felt sorry for her, and for himself, and in this nervously emotional, tender mood he walked out of the cabin where he was quartered with Nesvitsky and began pacing back and forth outside it.

The night was foggy, and through the mist the moonlight shimmered eerily. "Yes, tomorrow, tomorrow!" he thought. "Tomorrow everything may be over for me! All these memories will mean nothing — none of them will matter anymore. Tomorrow perhaps — almost certainly — I have a feeling that for the first time I'll have a chance to show everything I'm capable of." And in his imagination the battle unfolded: the defeat, the fighting concentrated at one crucial point, the hesitation of all the commanders. And then that glorious moment — that Toulon he had waited for so long — finally arrives. He states his views firmly and clearly to Kutuzov, to Weyrother, and to the Emperors. Everyone is struck by the brilliance of his analysis, but no one dares to carry it out, so he takes a regiment, a division — on the condition that no one interferes with his command — leads his division to the decisive point, and wins the victory single-handedly. "But death and suffering?" suggested another voice. Prince Andrew, however, did not answer that voice and continued dreaming of his triumphs. The plans for the next battle are drawn up by him alone. Officially he is still just an adjutant on Kutuzov's staff, but he does everything himself. The next battle is won by him alone. Kutuzov is removed, and he is appointed... "And then what?" asked the other voice. "If before that you're not wounded ten times over, or killed, or betrayed — then what?" "Well then," Prince Andrew answered himself, "I don't know what will happen and don't want to know, and can't know. But if I want this — want glory, want to be known, want to be loved — it's not my fault that I want it and want nothing else and live for nothing else. Yes, for that alone! I will never tell anyone this, but oh God! What am I supposed to do if I love nothing but glory and the esteem of others? Death, wounds, the loss of family — none of it frightens me. And dear as so many people are to me — my father, my sister, my wife — the people closest to me — yet terrible and unnatural as it seems, I would give them all up in an instant for one moment of glory, of triumph, of love from people I don't know and never will know — for the love of these men here," he thought, listening to voices in Kutuzov's courtyard. It was the orderlies packing up; one voice, probably a coachman's, was teasing Kutuzov's old cook, whom Prince Andrew knew — a man called Tit. "Tit, hey, Tit!" he was saying.
"What?" the old man replied.
"Go on, Tit, go thresh a bit!" said the joker.
"Oh, go to hell!" called out a voice, drowned by the laughter of the orderlies and servants.
"All the same, I love and value nothing but victory over them all — this mysterious power and glory that hovers here above me in the mist!"
